summary: KS3 pupils derive and apply a connected family of area formulae (parallelogram = base × perpendicular height; triangle = ½ base × perpendicular height; trapezium = ½(a+b) × perpendicular height) and the volume of any prism as cross-sectional area × length, with the cylinder as the special case V = πr²h. The core understanding is derivation from the rectangle rather than memorisation, and consistently using the PERPENDICULAR height (at right angles to the base), never a slanted side. The volume strand reduces to one idea: find the uniform cross-section, then extrude it along the length.
misconceptions: Using the slanted side instead of the perpendicular height for a parallelogram, triangle or trapezium
Dropping the ½ (triangle/trapezium) — applying the rectangle/parallelogram rule (base × height) to a triangle
Confusing area with perimeter (adding sides) or volume with surface area
Multiplying all the given lengths together for volume instead of cross-section × length
Muddling the units — cm² for volume, or forgetting square/cubic units

activities.title: Shear a parallelogram into a rectangle
steps: Study a parallelogram on a grid labelled with base 8 cm, a perpendicular height 5 cm marked with a right-angle symbol, AND a slant side 6 cm.
Before computing, decide which length should multiply the base to give the area, and say why.
Move the sloping triangular overhang from one end across to the other so the shape becomes a rectangle; confirm the covered area is unchanged.
State the area: 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (the 6 cm slant is a decoy and is not used).
If a dynamic model is available, drag the overhang live and watch an area readout stay constant as the parallelogram becomes a rectangle.
activities.insight: A parallelogram rearranges into a rectangle of the same base and the same PERPENDICULAR height, so its area is base × perpendicular height — the slant side is longer and is never the height.

activities.title: Halve the parallelogram to get the triangle
steps: Take the parallelogram (or rectangle) from the previous activity and draw a diagonal, splitting it into two congruent triangles.
Explain that one triangle is exactly half the parallelogram, so its area is ½ × base × perpendicular height.
Compute a triangle with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm: ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². Compare with the un-halved 6 × 4 = 24 cm² to see what the ½ corrects.
Mark the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol and check it is not the slanted edge.
activities.insight: A triangle is half of its surrounding parallelogram, so the ½ is not an arbitrary rule but a visible consequence of halving.

activities.title: Average the parallel sides of a trapezium
steps: Work with a trapezium with parallel sides a = 4 cm and b = 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm.
Find the average of the parallel sides: (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7 cm, and explain that the trapezium 'evens out' to a rectangle of width 7 and the same height.
Compute the area: ½(4 + 10) × 6 = 7 × 6 = 42 cm².
Explain in words why the formula uses 7 rather than 4 or 10.
If an adjustable model is available, drag the two parallel sides and watch a live ½(a+b)h readout update to feel how the average controls the area.
activities.insight: A trapezium's area equals the average of its parallel sides times the perpendicular height, because it levels out to an equivalent rectangle of that average width.

activities.title: Extrude a cross-section into a prism (and then a cylinder)
steps: Find the area of a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm: ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
Multiply by the length of the prism to get the volume: 12 × 10 = 120 cm³. Resist multiplying all three given lengths (6 × 4 × 10 = 240) — that would ignore the ½ and treat the prism as a cuboid.
State the single rule out loud: volume of any prism = area of the uniform cross-section × length.
Apply the same rule to a cylinder: with a circular cross-section of radius 3 cm, cross-section = π × 3² = 9π ≈ 28.3 cm², so volume = 9π × h, i.e. V = πr²h.
If a 3D model is available, rotate the prism and slice it to expose the constant cross-section, then extrude a circle into a cylinder to ground πr²h.
Check: investigate what happens to the volume if you double the length, versus if you double the cross-section area.
activities.insight: Cuboids, triangular prisms and cylinders are all the same idea — a cross-section extruded along a length — so volume is cross-section area × length, with the cylinder being the circular case πr²h.

activities.title: Area versus perimeter, and keeping units straight
steps: For one figure, compute both its perimeter (distance around, add the side lengths, linear units) and its area (covering, square units) and label each with the correct unit.
Say which quantity uses linear units (cm) and which uses square units (cm²); then state why a volume uses cubic units (cm³).
Apply the quick check: two lengths multiplied → square units; an area multiplied by a length → cubic units.
Deliberately spot and correct a worked example that reports a volume in cm² or an area with no unit.
activities.insight: Area measures covering (square units), perimeter measures going round (linear units), and volume measures filling (cubic units); the unit follows from how many lengths were multiplied.

activities.title: Consolidate with formula practice and distractors
steps: Match each shape (parallelogram, triangle, trapezium) to its area formula and each prism to the cross-section × length rule.
Complete missing parts of each formula from memory after having derived them.
Choose the correct area from options where one distractor multiplies by the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, and justify the rejection.
On a novel figure, state which measurement is the perpendicular height before computing.
activities.insight: Fluency with the formulae should coexist with the ability to reject slant-side distractors and to justify each choice, not just recall a rule.

checkQuestion: Give the child three figures with a ruler: (a) a parallelogram with base 8 cm, a perpendicular height of 5 cm marked with a right-angle symbol, AND a slant side of 6 cm labelled; (b) a trapezium with parallel sides 4 cm and 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm; (c) a triangular prism whose triangular cross-section has base 6 cm and height 4 cm, and length 10 cm. Set them to find (a) the area of the parallelogram, (b) the area of the trapezium and explain why the formula works, and (c) the volume of the prism. Then ask: 'if the cross-section were a circle of radius 3 cm instead, how would you find the volume?' Watch which length they use for height, whether they halve where needed, and whether they use cross-section × length for the volume.
checkAnswer: (a) 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (base × perpendicular height; the 6 cm slant is not used). (b) ½(4+10) × 6 = 42 cm², explained as the average of the parallel sides times the height (the trapezium 'evens out' to a rectangle of width 7). (c) cross-section area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm², volume = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³. For the cylinder: cross-section = π × 3² = 9π ≈ 28.3 cm², volume = 9π × h. Areas in cm², volume in cm³.
